Medicine.question: ১) Which is the most useful technique for assessing valvular heart disease?
Medicine.exp:
The correct answer is Doppler echocardiography. It is the most useful non-invasive technique for assessing valvular heart disease because it provides information about valve structure, severity of stenosis or regurgitation, pressure gradients, and blood flow velocity across valves.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • ECH (Echocardiography) – Conventional echocardiography assesses valve anatomy, but Doppler echocardiography provides additional haemodynamic assessment and is the preferred technique.

  • Coronary angiogram – Used mainly to assess coronary artery disease, not valve lesions.

  • PTMC (Percutaneous Transvenous Mitral Commissurotomy) – A treatment procedure for suitable cases of mitral stenosis, not a diagnostic assessment technique.

High-yield points:

  • Valvular heart disease assessment → Doppler echocardiography

  • Echocardiography → First-line investigation for valve disease

  • Doppler → Measures pressure gradient and severity of stenosis/regurgitation

Medicine.question: ২) ‘Pansystolic murmur in mitral area which radiates to left axilla’ - occurs in _____?
Medicine.exp:
The correct answer is mitral regurgitation (MR). MR produces a pansystolic (holosystolic) murmur best heard at the mitral area (apex), which typically radiates to the left axilla due to the direction of the regurgitant jet from the left ventricle to the left atrium.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Mitral stenosis (MS) – Produces a mid-diastolic rumbling murmur with an opening snap, best heard at the apex.

  • Aortic stenosis (AS) – Produces a systolic ejection murmur best heard at the right second intercostal space, radiating to the carotids.

  • Aortic regurgitation (AR) – Produces an early diastolic decrescendo murmur best heard along the left sternal border.

High-yield points:

  • MR → Pansystolic murmur → Apex → Radiates to left axilla

  • MS → Mid-diastolic rumble + opening snap

  • AS → Ejection systolic murmur → Carotid radiation

  • AR → Early diastolic murmur → Left sternal border

Medicine.question: ৩) Which is not true about Tricuspid regurgitation?
Medicine.option3: Pansystolic murmur in left parasternal area
Medicine.option4: murmur increases with standing position
Medicine.exp:
The correct answer is murmur increases with standing position. In tricuspid regurgitation, the murmur is a pansystolic murmur best heard at the left lower sternal border and becomes louder with inspiration (Carvallo sign) due to increased venous return to the right heart.

The other options are correct because:

  • Pulsatile liver – Occurs due to transmission of right ventricular systolic pressure into the hepatic veins.

  • Giant ‘v’ wave in JVP – A characteristic finding caused by systolic regurgitant flow into the right atrium.

  • Pansystolic murmur in left parasternal area – Typical auscultatory finding of tricuspid regurgitation.

High-yield points:

  • TR → Pansystolic murmur + giant v wave + pulsatile liver

  • TR murmur increases with inspiration

  • MR murmur → Apex radiating to left axilla

  • Carvallo sign → Increased right-sided murmurs during inspiration

Medicine.question: ৪) Which murmur is found in mitral stenosis?
Medicine.exp:
The correct answer is mid-diastolic murmur (MDM). Mitral stenosis causes obstruction of blood flow from the left atrium to the left ventricle during diastole, producing a characteristic low-pitched rumbling mid-diastolic murmur best heard at the apex, often with an opening snap.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • PSM (Pansystolic murmur) – Seen in mitral regurgitation and tricuspid regurgitation.

  • ESM (Ejection systolic murmur) – Seen in aortic stenosis and pulmonary stenosis.

  • EDM (Early diastolic murmur) – Seen in aortic regurgitation and pulmonary regurgitation.

High-yield points:

  • Mitral stenosis → Mid-diastolic rumbling murmur + opening snap

  • Mitral regurgitation → Pansystolic murmur radiating to left axilla

  • Aortic stenosis → Ejection systolic murmur radiating to carotids

  • Aortic regurgitation → Early diastolic decrescendo murmur

Medicine.question: ৫) Gallop rhythm is characteristic of _____?
Medicine.exp:
The correct answer is left ventricular failure (LVF). A gallop rhythm, especially an S3 gallop, is a classic finding in heart failure due to increased ventricular filling pressures and volume overload. It is commonly associated with left ventricular systolic dysfunction.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • RVF (Right ventricular failure) – May occasionally produce an S3 gallop, but it is less characteristic than LVF.

  • Mitral stenosis (MS) – Produces a mid-diastolic rumbling murmur with an opening snap, not a gallop rhythm.

  • Aortic stenosis (AS) – Produces an ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids, not a gallop rhythm.

High-yield points:

  • S3 gallop → Volume overload states (LV failure, dilated cardiomyopathy)

  • S4 gallop → Stiff ventricle (hypertension, aortic stenosis, HCM)

  • Gallop rhythm → Suggests ventricular dysfunction

Medicine.question: ৬) All of the following are cardinal signs of CCF except _____?
Medicine.exp:
The correct answer is pulmonary hypertension. The cardinal signs of congestive cardiac failure (CCF) include features of venous congestion, such as raised JVP (engorged neck veins), hepatomegaly (often tender), and dependent pitting oedema. Pulmonary hypertension is not considered a cardinal clinical sign of CCF.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Engorged and pulsatile neck veins – A sign of right-sided heart failure due to raised venous pressure.

  • Enlarged and tender liver – Occurs due to hepatic venous congestion in right heart failure.

  • Dependent pitting oedema – A common sign of systemic venous congestion.

High-yield points:

  • Right heart failure → Raised JVP + hepatomegaly + peripheral oedema

  • Left heart failure → Pulmonary congestion + dyspnoea + pulmonary oedema

  • CCF → Combination of systemic and/or pulmonary congestion due to cardiac dysfunction

Medicine.question: ৭) In malignant hypertension the diastolic BP is above _____ mmHg?
Medicine.exp:
The correct answer is 130 mmHg. Malignant hypertension is a severe form of hypertension characterized by a marked elevation of blood pressure, classically with diastolic blood pressure ≥130 mmHg, often associated with retinopathy (papilloedema), renal impairment, and other target-organ damage.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • 100 mmHg – Indicates hypertension but not malignant hypertension.

  • 110 mmHg – Represents severe hypertension but below the classical threshold for malignant hypertension.

  • 140 mmHg – Extremely high but not the standard diagnostic cutoff for malignant hypertension.

High-yield points:

  • Malignant hypertension → DBP ≥130 mmHg + target organ damage

  • Hypertensive emergency → Severe BP elevation with acute target organ injury

  • Fundoscopy → Papilloedema (grade IV hypertensive retinopathy) is a classic feature

Medicine.question: ৮) When there is no response to antihypertensive drugs, it is called _____?
Medicine.exp:
The correct answer is refractory hypertension. It refers to hypertension that remains uncontrolled despite the use of multiple antihypertensive medications, including appropriate combination therapy. It represents a more severe form of treatment failure than resistant hypertension.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Resistant hypertension – Hypertension that remains above target despite the use of three antihypertensive drugs of different classes (including a diuretic) at optimal doses.

  • Relative hypertension – Not a recognized clinical category.

  • Malignant hypertension – Severe hypertension associated with acute target-organ damage, such as papilloedema or renal injury.

High-yield points:

  • Resistant hypertension → Uncontrolled BP despite ≥3 drugs (including diuretic)

  • Refractory hypertension → Uncontrolled despite more intensive multidrug therapy

  • Malignant hypertension → Severe BP elevation + target organ damage

Medicine.question: ৯) Minor criteria for diagnosis of rheumatic fever excludes _____?
Medicine.exp:
The correct answer is polyarthritis. In the Jones criteria for diagnosis of rheumatic fever, polyarthritis is a major criterion, not a minor criterion.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Fever – A minor criterion.

  • Leukocytosis – May be associated with rheumatic fever and is considered a minor laboratory finding in some criteria sets.

  • High ESR – A minor criterion indicating inflammation.

High-yield points:

  • Major Jones criteria → JONES

    • Joint inflammation (migratory polyarthritis)

    • O (carditis)

    • Nodules (subcutaneous nodules)

    • Erythema marginatum

    • Sydenham chorea

  • Minor criteria → Fever, raised ESR/CRP, prolonged PR interval, previous rheumatic fever

  • Polyarthritis = Major criterion

Medicine.question: ১০) Which is not included in X-ray finding of mitral stenosis?
Medicine.exp:
The correct answer is oligemic lung field. In mitral stenosis, obstruction to left ventricular filling causes increased left atrial pressure, leading to pulmonary venous hypertension and pulmonary congestion, not reduced pulmonary blood flow.

The other options are features that may be seen in mitral stenosis:

  • Double contoured right heart border – Due to left atrial enlargement, producing a double density along the right heart border.

  • Mitral valve calcification – May occur in chronic rheumatic mitral stenosis.

  • Pulmonary venous hypertension – A common X-ray finding due to elevated left atrial pressure.

High-yield points:

  • Mitral stenosis X-ray → Left atrial enlargement + pulmonary venous hypertension + pulmonary congestion

  • Straightening of left heart border → Enlarged pulmonary artery/left atrial appendage enlargement

  • Oligemic lung fields → Seen in conditions with reduced pulmonary blood flow (e.g., Tetralogy of Fallot)

Medicine.question: ১১) What is the pulse of aortic stenosis?
Medicine.exp:
The correct answer is slow rising carotid pulse (pulsus parvus et tardus). In aortic stenosis, obstruction at the aortic valve limits left ventricular outflow, causing a slow upstroke and reduced amplitude of the carotid pulse.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Pulsus alternans – Seen in severe left ventricular failure due to alternating strong and weak ventricular contractions.

  • Collapsing pulse – Characteristic of aortic regurgitation due to rapid runoff of blood from the aorta into the left ventricle.

  • Pulsus bisferiens – Classically associated with hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy and sometimes combined aortic valve disease.

High-yield points:

  • Aortic stenosis → Slow rising, low-volume carotid pulse (pulsus parvus et tardus)

  • Aortic regurgitation → Collapsing pulse

  • HOCM → Pulsus bisferiens

  • Severe LV failure → Pulsus alternans

Medicine.question: ১২) Which is non-modifiable risk factors of coronary artery disease?
Medicine.exp:
The correct answer is genetic factors. Genetic predisposition is a non-modifiable risk factor for coronary artery disease (CAD), meaning it cannot be changed. A family history of premature CAD increases an individual's risk.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Hypertension – A modifiable risk factor that can be controlled with lifestyle changes and medication.

  • Smoking – A major modifiable risk factor for CAD.

  • Diabetes mellitus – Considered a modifiable metabolic risk factor through glycaemic control and lifestyle modification.

High-yield points:

  • Non-modifiable CAD risk factors → Age, sex, family history/genetics

  • Modifiable CAD risk factors → Smoking, hypertension, diabetes, dyslipidaemia, obesity, physical inactivity

Medicine.question: ১৩) Which is not cardiac enzyme?
Medicine.exp:
The correct answer is CKBB. CK-BB (creatine kinase brain type) is mainly found in the brain and smooth muscle and is not considered a cardiac enzyme marker.

The other options are associated with cardiac muscle injury:

  • LDH – Especially LDH-1 was historically used as a marker of myocardial infarction (though now largely replaced by troponins).

  • CK-MM – Present in skeletal muscle and also found in cardiac muscle.

  • CK-MB – A relatively cardiac-specific isoenzyme of creatine kinase and was commonly used for diagnosis of myocardial infarction.

High-yield points:

  • Most specific cardiac marker → Cardiac troponin I/T

  • CK-MB → Useful for detecting reinfarction due to early return to normal

  • CK-BB → Brain isoenzyme, not a cardiac marker

Medicine.question: ১৪) In case of MI which one appears 1st & last for a long time?
Medicine.exp:
The correct answer is Troponin I. In myocardial infarction (MI), troponin I rises early and remains elevated for the longest duration among the given cardiac biomarkers. It usually appears within 3–6 hours after myocardial injury and remains elevated for about 7–10 days.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • CK (especially CK-MB) – Rises early (3–6 hours) but returns to normal within 2–3 days, making it useful for detecting reinfarction.

  • LDH – Appears later (24–72 hours) and remains elevated for about 7–10 days, but it is not the earliest marker.

  • AST – Rises within 6–12 hours but returns to normal within a few days and is less specific.

High-yield points:

  • Earliest marker of MI → Myoglobin (not listed)

  • Most specific marker → Cardiac troponin I/T

  • Longest elevated → Troponin (7–10 days)

  • CK-MB → Best for reinfarction detection

Medicine.question: ১৫) Hypertension in pregnancy should be treated with _____?
Medicine.exp:
The correct answer is methyldopa. It is a commonly used and well-established antihypertensive drug in pregnancy because of its long safety record and lack of significant adverse fetal effects. It acts centrally by stimulating α2-adrenergic receptors, reducing sympathetic outflow.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Captopril – An ACE inhibitor and contraindicated in pregnancy due to risk of fetal renal damage, oligohydramnios, and other fetotoxic effects.

  • Amlodipine – May be used in some cases, but it is not the classic first-line answer for pregnancy hypertension.

  • Losartan – An angiotensin receptor blocker (ARB) and contraindicated in pregnancy due to fetal toxicity.

High-yield points:

  • Pregnancy hypertension drugs → Methyldopa, labetalol, nifedipine

  • Avoid in pregnancy → ACE inhibitors and ARBs

  • Methyldopa → Long safety experience in pregnancy

Medicine.question: ১৬) Which of the following is a cause of left heart failure?
Medicine.exp:
The correct answer is systemic hypertension. Chronic systemic hypertension increases the workload against which the left ventricle must pump, causing left ventricular hypertrophy and eventually left ventricular failure due to impaired relaxation and/or systolic dysfunction.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Anemia – Can cause a high-output cardiac failure, but it is not a typical primary cause of left heart failure.

  • Mitral stenosis – Primarily causes left atrial enlargement and pulmonary venous hypertension; the left ventricle is usually underfilled and not a common cause of left ventricular failure.

  • Pulmonary hypertension – Mainly causes right heart failure due to increased right ventricular afterload.

High-yield points:

  • Causes of left heart failure → Hypertension, ischemic heart disease, aortic stenosis, cardiomyopathy

  • Causes of right heart failure → Pulmonary hypertension, COPD, left heart failure

  • Mitral stenosis → Left atrial enlargement + pulmonary congestion

Medicine.question: ১৭) T inversion signifies _____?
Medicine.exp:
The correct answer is ischemia. T-wave inversion on ECG is a classic sign of myocardial ischemia due to abnormal ventricular repolarization caused by reduced blood supply to the myocardium.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Injury – Usually produces ST-segment elevation (acute myocardial injury).

  • Infarction – Classically associated with pathological Q waves due to myocardial necrosis.

  • Necrosis – Represented by persistent Q waves rather than isolated T-wave inversion.

High-yield points:

  • T-wave inversion → Ischemia

  • ST elevation → Acute myocardial injury

  • Pathological Q wave → Myocardial necrosis/infarction

  • ST depression → Subendocardial ischemia

Medicine.question: ১৮) What is the most dangerous complication of MI?
Medicine.exp:
The correct answer is ventricular fibrillation (VF). VF is the most dangerous and common fatal arrhythmia in the early phase of acute myocardial infarction. It causes ineffective ventricular contraction, leading to sudden cardiac arrest and death if not immediately treated.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Atrial fibrillation (AF) – May occur after MI but is less immediately life-threatening than VF.

  • Heart block – Can occur, especially with inferior MI, but is not the most common immediate fatal complication.

  • Cardiogenic shock – A severe complication of extensive MI due to pump failure, but VF is the classic immediate lethal complication.

High-yield points:

  • Early death after MI → Ventricular fibrillation

  • Large anterior MI → Cardiogenic shock risk

  • Inferior MI → AV block (due to RCA involvement)

  • VF → Most common cause of sudden death in the early hours of MI

Medicine.question: ১৯) Which antihypertensive is contraindicated in gout?
Medicine.exp:
The correct answer is thiazide diuretics. Thiazides (e.g., hydrochlorothiazide) can increase serum uric acid levels by reducing uric acid excretion in the kidney, which may precipitate or worsen gout attacks.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Loop diuretics – Can also increase uric acid levels, but thiazides are the classic antihypertensive drugs tested in relation to gout.

  • ACE inhibitors – Not contraindicated in gout.

  • ARBs – Most are not contraindicated; losartan is actually uricosuric and may reduce uric acid levels.

High-yield points:

  • Gout + hypertension → Avoid thiazides if possible

  • Losartan → ARB with uricosuric effect

  • Thiazides → Hyperuricaemia + gout risk

  • Loop diuretics → Also may cause hyperuricaemia

Medicine.question: ২০) What is the nature of apex beat in MS?
Medicine.exp:
The correct answer is tapping apex beat. In mitral stenosis (MS), the left ventricle is usually normal in size, but the palpable tapping apex beat occurs due to a palpable loud first heart sound (S1) caused by the forceful closure of a mobile mitral valve.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Thrusting apex beat – Suggests increased left ventricular volume overload, as seen in mitral regurgitation or other volume overload states.

  • Heaving apex beat – Indicates left ventricular pressure overload, classically seen in aortic stenosis or hypertension.

  • Thrill – A palpable murmur vibration, not a type of apex beat.

High-yield points:

  • Mitral stenosis → Tapping apex beat + loud S1 + opening snap

  • Aortic stenosis → Heaving apex beat

  • Mitral regurgitation → Displaced, thrusting apex beat
